annotation.reasoning_summary: The layer maps housing association-owned building/block footprints with attributes like corporation, dwelling counts, and construction period, so the main phenomenon is discrete housing objects, not a full tessellation or reporting-unit grid.
Point features marking individual archaeological cesspit/find spots; this is a set of discrete objects, not a measurement, event, or network.

Point features mark distinct archaeological find locations/objects (selective sites with addresses, images, object codes), so Geometry is PointDS and the main phenomenon is ObjectDS rather than amount or event.

Polygons mark selected archaeological site areas, not a complete area partition, so PlainVectorRegion fits. The layer represents bounded phenomenon zones with site records and descriptions, making it a PatchDS rather than reporting units or objects.

Polygon areas mark selected barbecue restriction/permission zones in parks, not a full tessellation or reporting unit. The decisive rule is bounded selected areas/patches, with isolated polygons supporting PlainVectorRegion.
Polygon areas represent selected conservation/protected historic districts, not a full tessellation or reporting units; the polygons are isolated bounded zones, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS.
Point features mark survey locations where wild bees were inventoried in specific years; the main phenomenon is observation occurrence over time, so PointDS + EventDS.
Point locations with x-aantal bijenkasten/bijenvolken; the main phenomenon is the numeric amount per location, so AmountDS rather than ObjectDS.
Polygons form a near-partition of Amsterdam soil-quality zones, and the layer is a full-area thematic classification by zone/function/quality, so VectorTessellation + CoverageDS.
Point features represent individual trees (named species, tree number, planting year, owner/manager), so this is a point object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point layer of individual trees; each feature is a distinct real-world object, with numeric fields as attributes rather than the main phenomenon.
Point layer of individual trees; each point is a distinct real-world object, not a measurement or event.
Point features represent individual trees with species, plant year, owner, and manager attributes; this is a discrete object layer, not an amount or event layer.
Point features marking discrete neighborhood compost initiatives at street locations; the main phenomenon is identifiable objects, not measurements or events.

Polygons are selected camera areas/overlast zones rather than a complete partition, so PlainVectorRegion fits; the named areas represent bounded phenomenon patches, not reporting units or full coverage.
Point locations of individual Canadian poplar trees; the layer is a discrete object inventory with attributes and management status, so ObjectDS rather than amount or event.
Point features represent individual crowd-monitoring sensors/telsystemen, i.e. discrete objects with attributes, not measurements or events.

The layer shows selected culture-historical area polygons, not a full administrative/reporting tessellation. The decisive entity rule is patch: bounded zones of cultural-historical value and protected areas, with numeric fields only as attributes.
Point features mark distinct knotweed sightings/occurrences with species and photo attributes, so this is an object layer on points rather than an amount or event layer.
Point map of ecopassage knelpunten/passages; each point represents a barrier or planned/realized mitigation case, so the decisive rule is EventDS for issues/actions occurring at locations.

Polygons are isolated wind-energy potential areas, not a full-area tessellation; the decisive entity rule is patch/selected zone rather than reporting unit or coverage. Numeric MW/output values are attributes of the wind sites, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Point layer of polling locations/stemlocaties with vote counts and percentages; the main phenomenon is electoral amounts at points, not the facilities themselves.
Point locations mark oak processionary caterpillar nest reports with mutation dates and statuses; the layer is real-time and changes over time, so EventDS on points.

Polygon areas mark selected pedicab restriction/allowance zones, not a full-area partition or reporting units. The main phenomenon is bounded regulatory patches (e.g., forbidden/allowed areas), so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS.
Point features represent pedicab and carriage stands, i.e. distinct real-world pitch locations; classified by object rather than amount, event, or measurement.
Point features represent individual non-residential BAG addresses/buildings with a classified function; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.

Polygon layer of block-street areas showing function-mix categories (WON/VZN/WRK) across built-up units; this is thematic full-area classification, but the polygons do not form a near-complete tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion + CoverageDS.
Neighborhoods are administrative/reporting units that partition the city, and the polygon topology strongly supports a tessellation.
Neighborhood/combinations polygons form an administrative tessellation of Amsterdam; codes and areas indicate reporting units, so use VectorTessellation + LatticeDS.

Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete administrative partition with high shared boundaries, and the layer is reporting units (buurten/wijken) with codes and area attributes, so VectorTessellation + LatticeDS.
Neighborhood polygons with codes and shared boundaries form a tessellation; they are reporting/statistical units, so LatticeDS.
City districts are reporting/administrative units, and the polygons form a tessellation of Amsterdam with high shared boundaries and adjacency; the area field is just an attribute.
City districts are administrative reporting units that partition the city area; the numeric area field is an attribute, not the main phenomenon.

Administrative/area units (Buurten, Wijken, Gebieden, Stadsdelen) form a near-complete partition, supported by strong shared boundaries and adjacency, so VectorTessellation. The features are reporting/aggregation areas with codes and area attributes, so LatticeDS.

The layer shows Amsterdam gebieds/wijken/stadsdelen polygons that partition the area, supported by tessellation topology hints. These are reporting/administrative units, so LatticeDS is the best entity match.

The layer is a set of Amsterdam practice areas/stadsdelen/wijken/gebieden that function as reporting units and form a near-complete partition; topology strongly supports tessellation, so the entity is LatticeDS.
Administrative/practice areas with names and codes form a tessellation of Amsterdam; they are reporting areas rather than objects, so LatticeDS with VectorTessellation.

The layer maps industrial noise zones/contours (50 dB, TERREIN) rather than reporting units or objects. Polygons represent contour bands/affected areas, so ContourDS; geometry is treated as PlainVectorRegion because these are selected noise zones, not a full partition.

Polygons are noise contour bands (55-60, 60-65, etc.), so the main phenomenon is interval/isoline classes rather than reporting units or objects; use contour regions. Topology hints and class bands support PlainVectorRegion rather than a full tessellation.
Noise contour polygons with class bands like 50-55 dB and >70 dB indicate contour/isoline zones rather than a reporting tessellation; the decisive rule is contour bands.

The layer shows noise contour polygons with decibel classes (e.g., 50-55 dB, 55-60 dB), so the main phenomenon is contour banding rather than reporting units or objects. Despite adjacency, the selected contour zones and overlap/selection cues fit a contour-region map, not a tessellation.
Point features represent polling/stem locations, and the main mapped phenomenon is vote counts/percentages by location rather than the places themselves, so PointDS + AmountDS.
Point layer of individual green roof locations with addresses and roof types; these are identifiable objects, not measurements or events.
Land use map with 8764 adjacent polygons forming a near-complete partition; categorical land-use classes indicate full-area thematic coverage, so this is a VectorTessellation with CoverageDS.
Point features represent selected historical building/archeological sites with names, functions, and dates; this is a set of identifiable objects, not an amount or event layer.

The layer depicts three selectable Amsterdam boundary shapes used for visual comparison, not a full partition or reporting grid, so PlainVectorRegion. The features are discrete municipal/metropolitan area objects, so ObjectDS rather than amount or coverage.

The layer maps selected dog-run, ban, and restriction zones rather than a full-area partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The decisive entity rule is PatchDS: bounded phenomenon areas with seasonal restriction zones, not reporting units, objects, or coverage.

Polygons represent selected green areas/managed zones in the Main Green Structure, not a full-area reporting unit or exhaustive classification; this fits bounded phenomenon patches. The layer is about protected green-area patches, not amounts.
Point features representing individual elm trees; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point layer of identifiable housing projects/buildings with names, addresses, owners, and unit counts; the main phenomenon is discrete objects, not the numeric amount.
Point features represent individual chestnut trees in a growing map; the species and damage status are attributes of each object, so this is ObjectDS on PointDS.
Point layer of sampled climate variables (Maaiveld, GLG, GLG_maaiveld) used to measure a continuous phenomenon; this fits PointMeasuresDS rather than objects or amounts.

Polygons form a near-complete thematic partition of Amsterdam flood risk zones, supported by high shared boundaries and adjacency, so VectorTessellation. The categories are probability and depth bands/classes for inundation, making it a contour-like interval classification rather than objects or amounts.
Point map of market locations (fixed sites/venues) with schedule and category attributes, so the decisive rule is point objects rather than amounts or events.
Point features represent discrete green monuments/bijzondere bomen sites, not measurements or events; the decisive rule is point ObjectDS.
Point layer of individually identifiable monumental trees; the decisive rule is object classification for discrete real-world assets, not AmountDS since numeric fields are just attributes.
Point layer of discrete monuments/buildings; the main phenomenon is identifiable heritage objects, not measurements or events.

Point features mark actual presence locations of rare wall plants; the main meaning is occurrence/presence, not measurement. The points are occurrence records with species attributes and yearly counts as secondary fields.

The layer shows NO2 measurements at monitoring locations, so the main phenomenon is sampled point measurements. Geometry is PointDS because it represents measurement points rather than regions or lines.
Point locations for NO2 monitoring stations/buoys; the main phenomenon is sampled air-quality measurement at points, so PointDS + PointMeasuresDS.

Polygon layer shows the Oergeul as a selected interpreted zone/patch, not a reporting unit or full-area coverage. Topology hints and description support PlainVectorRegion, and the main phenomenon is the bounded geological patch of the old tidal channel.
Point layer of borehole/sounding measurements; the main phenomenon is sampled geotechnical values at locations, so PointMeasuresDS.

These are named development neighbourhood polygons, but they do not form a full administrative/statistical partition of Amsterdam; they are selected project/area objects, so PlainVectorRegion + ObjectDS.
Point layer of identifiable public toilet facilities; the decisive rule is object/facility mapping, not the numeric fee attribute.

Polygons are neighborhood-like areas forming a near-complete partition, so VectorTessellation. The layer marks selected policy/condition zones for overnight/hotel restrictions rather than reporting units or full coverage, so PatchDS.
Polygons form a near-complete area partition for parking-standard zones, and the categorical Categorie field indicates a full-area thematic classification (coverage/tessellation).
These are discrete named parks/green spaces with area attributes, not a full tessellation. They represent identifiable bounded objects; the numeric area is just an attribute, so ObjectDS.
Postcode4 areas are reporting/statistical units that partition the city as a near-complete tessellation; the decisive rule is tessellation + reporting-unit (postcode) classification.

Postcode4 areas are reporting/statistical units forming a near-complete tessellation, supported by high shared boundaries and adjacency. The main feature is postcode regions, not the area value attribute.

Postcode6 parcel-like polygons are discrete postal areas with overlaps and do not form a clean full tessellation; the decisive rule is region geometry as PlainVectorRegion. The features primarily represent postcode objects/zones identified by Postcode6, not numeric amounts or reporting units.
LineString infrastructure network layer; named roads/links with transport priority categories, so the decisive rule is NetworkDS for connected route/transport systems.

Polygon layer for Amsterdam plus/hoofdnetten pedestrian priority areas; these are thematic zones, not a full tessellation. The categorical field and map description indicate an area-wide classification of network priority, so CoverageDS fits best.
Point layer of named locations/cameras/sensors; the decisive rule is point objects, not measurements or events. The privacy link is an attribute of each object, so ObjectDS.
Point features marked with labels for cameras/sensors or investigations; this is mainly a set of identifiable point objects, not a measurement or event layer.
Point features mark distinct car fleet scan/camera/sensor locations with names and addresses, so this is a set of objects at points, not a measurement or event layer.
Point layer of election polling/stem locations with circle sizes encoding vote totals/percentages; main phenomenon is numeric election amount at points, not just point objects.

Polygon regions mark selected rainproof drainage problem areas/locations, not a full reporting tessellation; the layer is a bounded phenomenon patch with categorical drainage status, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS.
Polygons are isolated hydro problem/solution zones, not a full partition or reporting unit, and the layer represents bounded Rainproof vulnerability/knelpunt areas rather than objects or coverage.

The polygons are isolated bottleneck zones for rainproof problem areas, not a full tessellation or reporting units. The decisive entity rule is patch: selected affected areas with urgent water-overlap risk, not objects or coverage.

Polygons mark discrete Rainproof problem/impact locations rather than a reporting-unit tessellation; topology is sparse and the layer is a set of selected bounded zones, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS.

Point layer of identifiable religious buildings/places (churches, mosques, temples) with names and addresses, so Geometry is PointDS and the main phenomenon is discrete objects, not amounts or events.

Line features named by street/sidewalk segments indicate a connected route/infrastructure system; the key rule is network over object. Width and obstacle fields are attributes of sidewalk segments, not the main phenomenon itself.
LineString features describing roadway segments and directions for the moped-roadway decision; this is a connected transport/traffic route system, so LineDS + NetworkDS.

Points represent discrete public sports facilities/playgrounds (named locations like basketball courts), so PointDS and ObjectDS apply; numeric area is just an attribute, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Point locations of city farming sites with names, addresses, and categories; this is a set of identifiable real-world objects, not a measurement or event layer.

These are discrete city farming sites with names, addresses, and websites, so the layer represents identifiable bounded objects rather than a tessellation or area-wide coverage. The polygons are isolated patches, and the suggested region geometry is PlainVectorRegion.

Point features mark where space-seekers settled through the city pilot; the key meaning is an occurrence/placement over time (9 years), so EventDS. Geometry is PointDS from the Point feature collection.
Major streets are a connected road system, so the decisive rule is network. The geometry is LineDS because all features are LineString routes rather than regions or points.
Line geometry for district heating/cooling transport lines; the decisive rule is network/infrastructure, not the categorical status fields.

The layer depicts district heating/cooling network zones as buffered polygons, not a full partition. The decisive entity rule is network infrastructure (heat/cold networks), even though transport lines are simplified into polygons.

These are discrete housing plan project polygons, not a full tessellation; the layer maps identifiable planned development objects with attributes like project name and max dwelling count, so ObjectDS with PlainVectorRegion.
Point map of named local food/street farming initiatives and businesses with addresses and categories; these are discrete objects, not measurements or events.
Line geometry with tram and metro routes; metadata explicitly describes a transport network, so this is a NetworkDS.
LineString features represent the tram/metro route system; metadata explicitly says it is the network of stations, stops, and lines, so this is a NetworkDS layer.
Point features represent tram stops and metro stations in a connected transport system, so this is a point-based network layer rather than a measurement or object layer.
Point layer of tram stops and metro stations; the map description emphasizes the tram/metro network and stops, so the decisive rule is network infrastructure, with point geometry for stations/halts.

Point features represent distinct traffic-light-controlled intersections, not measurements or events. The decisive rule is point objects: each record is a real-world crossed junction with attributes like status and year installed.
Line network of road links, but the main mapped phenomenon is traffic prognoses/volumes on each link, so LineDS + AmountDS.
Point layer of voting locations; circles encode vote totals/percentages as the main phenomenon, so this is PointDS with AmountDS.
Point features represent individual trees identified by species, tree ID, planting year, and size classes; this is a discrete object layer, not an amount or event layer.
Point features represent discrete traffic information system objects (cameras, displays, polls, barriers) with identifiers and locations; this is an object layer, not an amount or event layer.
Point features represent discrete traffic information system objects/facilities, not measurements or events; object rule applies.
Point locations mark discrete breeding/nest sites for birds, with street and house-number attributes; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point features represent individual benches in Vondelpark, a set of identifiable real-world objects. The Boolean adoption status is an attribute, not the main phenomenon.

Line geometries represent street segments/sidewalk street sections, so LineDS. The layer maps walkability and sidewalk width conditions for discrete street segments rather than a network flow or amount layer, so ObjectDS.
Point features mark individual wall art objects at specific building addresses; this is an object inventory, not measurements or events.

Polygons form a near-complete citywide partition with strong shared boundaries, and the layer is a thematic classification of Amsterdam areas into welstand (amenity/design) levels, so this is tessellated coverage.

Polygons form a near-complete citywide partition with high shared boundaries, so VectorTessellation. The layer maps Amsterdam welstand systems, a full-area thematic classification of area categories, so CoverageDS.
Point features mark WWII incidents/occurrences at locations with dates and descriptions; this is a point event layer, not an object or measurement layer.

These are discrete housing project polygons, not a full-area reporting tessellation. The layer maps identifiable project areas with planned dwelling counts as attributes, so the decisive rule is object/ project polygons rather than amount or coverage.
Point layer of discrete do-it-yourself plot/project locations; each point represents a real-world plot or development object, not a measurement or event.

Polygon layer of all building roofs/daks across Amsterdam forms a near-complete citywide partition, and the Categorie field is a full-area thematic classification of solar-panel suitability on heritage roofs, so this is a tessellation with coverage.
Point features represent detected solar panel systems as discrete objects; numeric fields are attributes (panel count and wattpeak), so this is PointDS + ObjectDS rather than AmountDS.
Point features mark named swimming and play-water locations; this is a set of distinct places/facilities, so the decisive rule is object points, not amounts or events.
